Does Coca-Cola's cash cover its dividend?

In 2025, Coca-Cola paid $2.04 a share in dividends against $1.23 of free cash flow per share: 166%. In 2024, 175%. Free cash flow is the cash left after running the business and investing in it; above 100%, the dividend cost more than the cash the year produced.

How much dividend will I get?

Multiply the amount you invest by the dividend yield, or the shares you own by the dividend per share. At Coca-Cola's 2.3% yield, $10,000 pays about $230 a year before tax, about $19 a month.

Amount × yield = dividends a year

$10,000 × 2.3% = $230

Shares × dividend per share (2025)

100 × $2.04 = $204

For $1,000 a month: a year ÷ yield

$12,000 ÷ 2.3% = $521,739

The last line is before tax, and holds only if the yield stays at 2.3%.

The yield is a year of dividends divided by the share price. Yield in the report: 2.3%. Dividends paid in 2025: $2.04, or $2.04 ÷ $91.18 = 2.24% of the price. When the price falls, the yield rises, even if the dividend does not change.

Dividend reinvestment (DRIP) calculator: what does reinvesting change?

Reinvested dividends buy more shares, which pay dividends in turn. Over 10 years in Coca-Cola, if the dividend keeps growing 5.1% a year, as it did from 2021 to 2025, and the share price stays at $91.18:

  • Reinvested: $10,000 becomes $13,321.86 of shares; the dividends reach $463.93 a year.
  • Taken in cash: you keep $10,000 of shares, are paid $2,910.59 in all, and the dividends reach $360.81 a year.

How is it calculated?

The pre-filled yield is the one in our latest report on the company, on the share price of the date shown. The growth rate is the yearly change in dividends paid per share over the last five fiscal years. A company whose figures do not agree with each other is not pre-filled.

Each year it pays that yield on the value at the start of the year, raised by the dividend growth and lowered by any share-price growth you enter; with reinvestment on, the dividends after tax buy more shares at year end.

Excerpts from the report

1. The business

The Coca-Cola Company, or KO, owns beverage brands and earns money by selling their ingredients and finished drinks around the world. Its central economic idea is simple: KO creates demand for the brand, while a network of bottlers often makes, packages and delivers the drink.

3. History and capital decisions

In 2025, shareholder payments exceeded free cash flow because operating cash included a final fairlife acquisition payment of roughly $6.1 billion. In 2024, a roughly $6.0 billion tax-dispute payment depressed cash flow. Removing such events can clarify the ordinary business, but the payments still happened. Coca-Cola must therefore cover owners and investments across several normal years, not just in an adjusted calculation.

The 2025 fairlife payment reduced cash flow by $6.1 billion; without it, dividends and buybacks consumed 82.8% of free cash flow.

6. Valuation and the stock

Consider an illustration. An investor wants an 8% annual return and receives a first-year dividend equal to today’s 2.3% yield. If the shares sell for 20 times earnings after ten years, roughly 9% annual growth would make the dividends and sale price worth about today’s price. At 7% growth, the same assumptions produce a value of roughly $79 a share.

8. Where the price could go

The base dividend rises from $2.18 per share in October 2027 to $2.26 in 2028 and $2.34 in 2029. The bear case freezes the annualized payment at $2.12, reflecting cash-flow pressure. The bull case reaches $2.45 by 2029 because stronger cash generation permits faster increases.

Cash generation will determine whether dividends and buybacks remain supportive. The forecast favors modest dividend growth because 2026 free cash flow guidance is at least $13.0 billion, but a renewed cash shortfall or adverse IRS resolution would reduce flexibility.
